posts.name: Tushar Verma
posts.cooked:
Hi,

Can you please explain why file1 and file2 are empty when wc fails? This is not the case when wc succeeds. Pls refer to the image below.

Screenshot from 2024-10-22 06-04-26966×544 49.5 KB

Thanks and regards,
Tushar Verma

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
Let me simplify the code to make it easier to understand:

~ (15) > echo "hello" | tee file1 | wc -l
1
~ (16) > cat file1
───────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       │ File: file1
───────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   1   │ hello
───────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
~ (16) > echo "hello" | tee file1 | wc -lo
wc: invalid option -- 'o'
Try 'wc --help' for more information.
                                                                                           1
~ (16) > cat file1
───────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       │ File: file1   <EMPTY>
───────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
~ (16) >

Pipes send data line by line into the next command. Some command such as grep, sed, wc etc work on a line by line basis, that is, they start processing a line as soon as it comes from the stdin, they do not wait for the entire input to finish and then start. Pipes also are blocking in nature, meaning the sender will wait till the receiver is ready and has received one line to send the next line.

wc when ran with a wrong argument even refuses to read the first line from stdin, which is actually a pipe. It terminates, since the flag used is wrong.

This sends a SIGPIPE signal from the reader wc to the writer tee of the pipe.
Usually when a SIGPIPE signal is sent, the process terminates, since it knows that whatever it wants to output, there is no one there to read it (on the right of the pipe).

tee also works line by line, and since it cannot output the first line to its stdout, it doesn’t write it to the files either and terminates.

Read more about it here

Hope it helps,
Thank you for bringing up good conceptual questions in this forum, hope it helps others too.

posts.name: Tushar Verma
posts.cooked:
Thank you for the detailed explanation.

sayan:

wc when ran with a wrong argument even refuses to read the first line from stdin, which is actually a pipe. It terminates, since the flag used is wrong.

This sends a SIGPIPE signal from the reader wc to the writer tee of the pipe.

sayan:

tee also works line by line, and since it cannot output the first line to its stdout, it doesn’t write it to the files either and terminates.

So basically, wc -lo being an invalid command sends SIGPIPE to tee and the process terminates. No lines are read by wc.

Question1
However for wc -lo to run, tee must finish and send an output (stdout), since these are in a pipe. stdout for tee points to the files and wc. So the files should have data written in them. But they don’t. Why?

Question2
SIGPIPE is sent incase of wc -lo but not incase of ls \blah i.e,

ls $HOME \blah | tee file1 file2 | ls \blah
doesn’t give a SIGPIPE. Files are populated in this case.

I assume this is because ls ran successfully although it didn’t have anything to show since \blah doesn’t exist.
Does that mean -
ls: cannot access '\blah': No such file or directory
is not an error message? It would not have a 0 return code (i think it will have a return code 2). Despite having non-zero return code, SIGPIPE is not sent. Could you pls shed some light on this?

I hope I could articulate my question well, pls let me know if more info is needed.

Thanks and regards,
Tushar Verma

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
Great doubts.

TusharVerma:

Question1
However for wc -lo to run, tee must finish and send an output (stdout), since these are in a pipe. stdout for tee points to the files and wc. So the files should have data written in them. But they don’t. Why?

Your understanding of pipes is not correct.

tee | wc

does not mean tee runs, does its job, finishes, then output everything to wc and wc starts.
As I mentioned in my original reply, pipes redirect output line by line, it does not store entire output in memory waiting for the program to finish and then passing on. It is literally as if the command’s output is attached to the next command’s input with a PVC pipe. It does not run one by one in a blocking manner.

(side note, this is the reason the infamous fork bomb :(){ : | : & } works.)

Bash runs both the tee command and wc commands, and ties tee’s output to wc’s input. (stdout and stdin).

tee can only run for even one line if the reciever of the pipe (wc) is ready to read the first line.

You can verify this yourself, or refer to this small demo I came up with:

image1630×1220 101 KB

You can observe that we have created two scripts.
sender.sh simply prints 0 to 5 to the stdout with a one second delay after each number.

If we run this directly using ./sender.sh we see it prints one number at a time.

If we want to first run sender.sh, get its entire output and then pass it to the receiver.sh, we can run it as follows:

❯ input=$(./sender.sh)
❯ ./reciever.sh <<< "$input"
0
1
2
3
4

Observe that the first command takes 5 seconds with no output, and then the second command runs instantly and prints all the numbers.

However, now we are redirecting its output to receiver.sh, which is a script that simply prints what came to its stdin to its stdout, its an stream identity process.

But observe that when we run sender.sh | receiver.sh that the output is printing each number one by one, and not all at once.

This proves that both the processes are running paralelly, and the fast process automatically is blocked and waits till the slow process produces a new line for the consumer to consume.

Thus wc does not run after tee is ran, they are run parallely, and as wc has wrong arguments it dies and closes the pipe, this causes tee to die prematurely as no one is reading what it is writing (as per previous reply).

TusharVerma:

Question2
SIGPIPE is sent incase of wc -lo but not incase of ls \blah i.e,

It is mostly speed and luck, as I said the processes are run paralelly, so if tee writes the first line before ls sends SIPIPE then it is stored, however if tee is slower than the SIGPIPE sent by ls then it wont write any line to output.

Try this (and play around with this)

~ (17) > for i in {1..10}; do echo $i; sleep 1; done | tee file | ls \blah
ls: cannot access 'blah': No such file or directory
                                                                                           2
~ (17) > cat file
───────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       │ File: file   <EMPTY>
───────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The sender is slow, thus the SIGPIPE stops tee from saving anything.

However,

~ (17) > for i in {1..10}; do echo $i; sleep 1; done | tee file | ls /
bin   dev  home  lib32  libx32      media  opt   root  sbin  srv  tmp  var
boot  etc  lib   lib64  lost+found  mnt    proc  run   snap  sys  usr
~ (17) > cat file
───────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       │ File: file
───────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   1   │ 1
───────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Here we are printing all contents of /, which takes some time, so ls terminates after the first 1 is printed. Observe the script still sleeps for 1 second. but the later numbers are not printed because ls still terminates (ls does not read stdin so it will simply do its job or printing whatever directory is in the args, sucess or error, and then terminate) and when ls terminates again the PIPE is broken so a SIGPIPE is sent to tee and inturn, to the producer, so the for loop stops.

Hope this clarifies the doubts. These are really interesting doubts and a very common misconception when starting out with shell. Glad these are being discussed.
